text: You get an array nums of unique integers. Return all possible subsets, the power set. No duplicate subsets. Any order is fine.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — the empty subset counts, and so does the full array. The order of subsets doesn't matter, and the order inside one subset doesn't matter either. Is that right? Since all values are distinct, there are exactly two to the n subsets. Each element is either in or out.
Are there any constraints on the input size?
n is between one and ten, each value is between negative ten and ten, and all values are distinct.

OK. So at most two to the tenth, which is one thousand twenty-four subsets, with five thousand one hundred twenty elements in total. The output itself is the cost, so I can't beat its size. I just need to build each subset once. Let me run through the example. One, two, three gives eight subsets: the empty one, three of size one, three of size two, and the full one, two, three. And a single zero gives the empty set and zero.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to loop a bitmask from zero to two to the n minus one, and build each subset from its bits. That works, and I'll use it later as a checker. This problem reminds me of the classic backtracking template. I keep a path, the current subset. I add one element, recurse, then take it back out. It fits because every subset is just a chain of choices, and backtracking walks each chain exactly once.

Here's the plan. One: record the path at the start of every call. Two: loop i from s to the end; push nums at i and recurse with i plus one, so the next pick comes after i. Three: pop it back before the next sibling. Here, I'm using s to keep track of where I may start picking. Every subset is built in increasing index order, so two, one can never appear. That's how I avoid duplicates. One thing worth flagging — I record path at every node, not only at the bottom. The root is the empty set, and each child adds one element with a bigger index. So the tree has exactly two to the n nodes, one per subset. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. The main function makes an empty answer and an empty path, and calls dfs from index zero. Dfs records the path, then loops: push, recurse with i plus one, pop. There's no base case. When s equals n, the loop doesn't run, and the call just returns. ans is a reference, so every call writes into the same list. One thing worth flagging — here path is passed by value. So each call gets its own copy, and the callee can't break the caller's path.
This works. Can you avoid copying path on every call?

Yes. I change one character: pass it by reference. Let me walk through that. Now there is one shared path for the whole tree. Every push back must be undone by the pop back after the call returns. Then the path is back to what it was, and the next sibling starts clean. There's a trade-off here. Copying path into ans happens in both versions. That copy is the output, so I can't skip it. By value just adds one more copy per call. At n equals ten, that's five thousand one hundred twenty extra elements copied. At n equals twenty, it's about ten and a half million extra, and I measured about one hundred twenty-two milliseconds versus one hundred four. Same big-O, but by reference is cheaper.

Let's dry-run the code with one, two, three — expected eight subsets. The call that matters is number five: after one, two, three is recorded, two pops bring the path back to just one, and the loop pushes three to record one, three. Eight calls, eight subsets — the same set as the official answer, in a different order. One thing worth flagging — pop back is needed even by value. The copy only protects the caller; inside one call, the loop keeps using its own copy. Without the pop, one, two gives one, two twice, instead of two. Corner cases: a single zero gives the empty set and zero. By reference without the pop, one, two gives one, two, two. Recursing with s plus one reuses the two. Recording only when s equals n loses the empty set on every input.

Let me think about complexity here. The time complexity is n times two to the n. There are two to the n subsets, and copying each one into ans costs up to n. That's the output size, so no solution can do better. The space complexity is linear extra by reference: the recursion stack and the path are at most n deep, not counting the output. By value it's n squared, since each of the n levels holds its own copy. In the worst-case scenario, n equals ten: one thousand twenty-four subsets and five thousand one hundred twenty output elements. It ran in zero point zero seven milliseconds by reference and zero point one by value. I also checked both versions against the bitmask on three thousand six hundred nineteen small arrays, with zero mismatches.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You saw that every node is a subset, so you record before the loop. You knew that pop back is needed even by value, and showed one, two coming out twice as proof. And you explained the by-value versus by-reference cost: the copy into ans stays, only the per-call copy goes. Good work.
